title: Κάμηλος ⟨ἀφοδεύσασα ἐν ποταμῷ⟩
titleEn: The Camel that Dunged in the River
part: The Camel that Dunged in the River (Chambry 144)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 144. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A camel was crossing a river running swiftly.
sentences.n: ὀξύ is an adverbial accusative with the participle, "running sharp", hence swiftly; ῥέοντα agrees with ποταμόν, not with the camel. κάμηλος is feminine here, as the participles that follow show. Chambry supplies the descriptive half of the title in angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ — his mark for words he adds.

sentences.t: Ἀφοδεύσασα δὲ καὶ τὴν κόπρον εὐθὺς ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῆς ἰδοῦσα διὰ τὸ ὀξὺ τοῦ ῥεύματος εἶπεν· « Τί τοῦτο ;
sentences.tr: Aphodeusasa de kai tēn kopron euthys emprosthen autēs idousa dia to oxy tou rheumatos eipen· « Ti touto ;
sentences.l: And having voided, and having seen the dung at once in front of her, because of the sharpness of the current, she said: « What is this?
sentences.i: And she relieved herself, and saw the dung straight away in front of her, carried ahead by the swiftness of the current, and said: « What is this?
sentences.n: διὰ τὸ ὀξὺ τοῦ ῥεύματος — a neuter adjective under the article with a genitive after it is the standard Greek way of naming a quality: "the sharpness of the stream". Τί τοῦτο has no verb at all; ἐστί is left out, as it constantly is. Chambry sets a space before the question mark.

sentences.t: τὰ ὄπισθέν μου ἔμπροσθέν μου νῦν ὁρῶ διερχόμενα. »
sentences.tr: ta opisthen mou emprosthen mou nyn horō dierchomena. »
sentences.l: the things behind me I now see passing in front of me. »
sentences.n: ὁρῶ takes the supplementary participle διερχόμενα for what is seen happening — a verb of perceiving takes a participle where a verb of saying would take an infinitive. ὄπισθεν and ἔμπροσθεν are adverbs pressed into service as noun-phrases under the article (τὰ ὄπισθεν, "the things behind"); each carries an extra acute thrown back on it by the enclitic μου that follows.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι] ἐν πόλει ⟨ἐν⟩ ᾗ ἔσχατοι καὶ ἄφρονες κρατοῦσιν ἀντὶ τῶν πρώτων καὶ φρονίμων ἁρμόζει ὁ μῦθος.
sentences.tr: [Hoti] en polei ⟨en⟩ hēi eschatoi kai aphrones kratousin anti tōn prōtōn kai phronimōn harmozei ho mythos.
sentences.l: [That] the fable fits a city ⟨in⟩ which the last and the senseless hold power in place of the first and the prudent.
sentences.i: The fable fits a city in which the last and the senseless hold power in place of the first and the prudent.
sentences.n: The two kinds of bracket sit on the same line and mean opposite things. [Ὅτι] Chambry judges interpolated and deletes; the sentence has its own governing verb in ἁρμόζει, so the idiomatic line stands on its own and does not supply the "the story shows" that an unbracketed bare Ὅτι calls for. ⟨ἐν⟩ is the other mark — a word Chambry adds, here to complete ἐν ᾗ, "in which". ἔσχατοι, "the last", answers πρῶτοι, "the first": the camel's back-to-front river turned into a description of a city.
